question: What is the main goal of giving medications for chronic, degenerative diseases like Parkinson's or Alzheimer's?

options.A: To manage ongoing physical and mental decline
options.B: To completely cure the underlying genetic defect
options.C: To permanently stop the normal aging process
options.D: To wipe out sudden bacterial infections in the tissues

explanation: You've got this! Because degenerative diseases cause gradual wear and tear on the body, medications are used to slow things down and help patients manage daily life, rather than providing a quick cure. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T19#GNS222_U4_T19_h1)

question: Why is treating a degenerative illness very different from treating a sudden bacterial infection?

options.A: Medications for degenerative conditions never have side effects
options.B: Infection drugs kill the invading germs, while degenerative drugs manage long-term loss
options.C: Infections are genetic, while degenerative diseases are caught from other people
options.D: Infections need lifelong management while degenerative diseases need short antibiotics

explanation: Spot on! An antibiotic can knock out an infection completely, but chronic degenerative conditions need ongoing care because the body's tissues are slowly breaking down over time. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T19#GNS222_U4_T19_h1)

question: What is the main purpose of a 'disease-modifying' drug?

options.A: To replace lost vitamins in the bloodstream
options.B: To give instant relief from sudden, sharp pain
options.C: To slow down how fast the disease damages the body
options.D: To completely cure the genetic mutation

explanation: Great job! Disease-modifying drugs don't fix everything overnight, but they work behind the scenes to alter the disease process and protect cells from further damage. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T19#GNS222_U4_T19_h2)

question: A patient asks why their new medicine isn't making them feel better right away, even though the doctor says it's working. What should you tell them?

options.A: The patient must be taking the wrong dose for their weight
options.B: Medications only work if you drink lots of cold water with them
options.C: Disease-modifying drugs focus on slowing future damage rather than instant relief
options.D: The drug is probably fake and should be thrown away

explanation: Well done! It's completely normal for patients to feel confused by this. Remind them that these medications are playing the long game—protecting their future health rather than giving an instant energy boost. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T19#GNS222_U4_T19_h2)

question: What is the primary goal of prescribing symptomatic medications in degenerative conditions?

options.A: To improve patient comfort and daily functioning
options.B: To stop all future cell death in the brain
options.C: To completely cure the underlying chronic illness
options.D: To permanently reverse any genetic mutations

explanation: You nailed it! When a disease can't be cured yet, our nursing focus shifts to easing symptoms so the patient can stay comfortable and independent for as long as possible. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T19#GNS222_U4_T19_h3)

question: Why might a patient with a degenerative nerve disease be given an antidepressant along with their other medications?

options.A: Coping with a life-changing chronic illness often takes a heavy emotional toll
options.B: Sadness is the physical cause of nerve cell breakdown
options.C: Depression medications help the liver process other pills faster
options.D: Antidepressants act as a direct cure for muscle weakness

explanation: Spot on! Caring for the whole person means looking after their mind as well as their body. Chronic illnesses are tough emotionally, and good mental health support is a vital part of nursing care. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T19#GNS222_U4_T19_h3)

question: What term describes the way the body absorbs, distributes, metabolizes, and gets rid of a drug?
explanation: Great memory! Think of pharmacokinetics as 'what the body does to the drug' as it travels through absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T19#GNS222_U4_T19_h4)

question: Why are older adults with degenerative conditions at a higher risk for drug toxicity?

options.A: Their digestive tracts destroy all medications before absorption
options.B: They always take their pills at the wrong time of day
options.C: Their brains actively attract and store extra chemical compounds
options.D: Their liver and kidney functions naturally slow down with age

explanation: You got it! Because the liver and kidneys clear drugs from the body, when they age and slow down, medications can build up and lead to accidental toxicity. Always start low and go slow with older adults! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T19#GNS222_U4_T19_h4)

question: Which health check is most crucial before giving oral medications to a patient with advanced neurological degeneration?

options.A: Checking how much water they drank today

explanation: Wonderful clinical thinking! Patients with advanced neurological issues often struggle with swallowing (dysphagia). Always check if they can safely swallow before handing over any pills to prevent choking or aspiration. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T19#GNS222_U4_T19_h5)

question: A patient with Parkinson's disease cannot swallow large pills, and their prescribed capsule is extended-release. What is the safest nursing action?

options.A: Crush the capsule into powder and mix it with food
options.B: Open the capsule and dissolve the beads in hot water
options.C: Consult the pharmacist or doctor for an alternative liquid or formulation
options.D: Skip the dose completely until their swallowing gets better

explanation: Spot on! Never crush extended-release medications because it ruins the special coating, causing all the medicine to flood the body at once and risking a dangerous overdose. Always talk to pharmacy! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T19#GNS222_U4_T19_h5)

question: Why can it be so tricky to spot a drug side effect in someone with a degenerative disease?

options.A: Patients with degenerative illnesses never tell anyone how they feel
options.B: Lab tests can never detect drug levels in chronic illnesses
options.C: Drug side effects always cause a sudden skin rash
options.D: Side effects like tremors or confusion can easily look like the disease getting worse

explanation: You're doing great! It's a classic clinical puzzle: if a drug causes shakiness or confusion, it's easy to assume the disease is simply progressing, when the patient might actually just need a medication adjustment. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T19#GNS222_U4_T19_h6)

question: Which lab tests are most important to monitor regularly for patients taking long-term multi-drug therapy?

options.A: Liver enzymes and kidney function tests
options.D: Complete blood count and blood type

explanation: Spot on! Since the liver and kidneys do the heavy lifting of processing and clearing drugs, keeping an eye on their lab values is our best way to catch early signs of strain or toxicity. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T19#GNS222_U4_T19_h6)

question: What is a major danger if a patient suddenly stops taking their long-term degenerative medications without talking to a doctor?

options.A: A sudden, severe return of symptoms or withdrawal
options.B: An immediate boost in liver and kidney function
options.C: Complete regeneration of normal nerve cells
options.D: An instant and permanent cure of the disease

explanation: You got it! Stopping chronic meds cold turkey can send the body into a severe rebound, making symptoms much worse than they were before. Tapering is usually needed! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T19#GNS222_U4_T19_h7)

question: A family caregiver is overwhelmed because their relative with memory loss keeps missing doses and mixing up pill times. What is the most helpful nursing intervention?

options.A: Tell the caregiver to stop giving all medications immediately
options.B: Warn them that missing doses has zero effect on chronic illnesses
options.C: Advise them to let the patient manage everything independently
options.D: Suggest practical tools like a labeled pill organizer and a daily schedule

explanation: Brilliant nursing advice! Simple organizational tools like pill boxes, alarms, and visual charts can lift a huge weight off family caregivers and keep patients safe on their medication routine. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T19#GNS222_U4_T19_h7)
